title: Slime Mold: 0% Mold, 100% Amazing
summary: Josh and Chuck explore slime molds, which are not animals, fungi, or true molds but protists. They cover their ancient origins, feeding by phagotrophy, their role in the food web, giant plasmodial slime molds, cellular slime molds that aggregate and sacrifice themselves to form fruiting stalks, and how they move via oscillating cytoplasm. The episode covers Japanese experiments in which Physarum polycephalum solved mazes and reproduced the Tokyo rail network and Roman roads using oat flakes, Lee Siegel and Evelyn Fox Keller's early work on cAMP signaling, bottom-up decision making and its relevance to AI and nanotechnology, habituation and memory experiments with a salt bridge, and Sage Jensen's slime mold algorithm being used to model the cosmic web of galaxies. The episode ends with a listener mail about the game Night Trap and Double Switch.

segments.title: Opening banter and what slime mold is
segments.summary: The hosts introduce slime mold, say it is not an animal, fungus, or true mold but a protist, and describe its appearance, slow movement, billion-year history, and phagotrophic feeding on bacteria, mold, and yeast.

segments.title: Slime mold as food, size, and plasmodial slime molds
segments.summary: They discuss the Mexican dish Coca de Luna, which is reportedly made from slime mold, the food web role of slime molds, and giant plasmodial slime molds that are one large multinucleate cell without cell walls.

segments.title: Cellular slime molds and aggregation
segments.summary: Cellular slime molds are single-celled organisms that join together when food is scarce, retain their cell walls, and move as a swarm, which makes them harder for predators to eat.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break with a brief host exchange.

segments.title: Altruism and Dictyostelium stalk formation
segments.summary: Some Dictyostelium discoideum cells sacrifice themselves to form a cellulose stalk that lifts spores, allowing passing animals to carry them away. Some cells also detach and die to save the group from infection.

segments.title: Movement and oat flake maze experiments
segments.summary: Slime molds move toward food by flowing cytoplasm. Toshiyuki Nakagaki's maze experiment with Physarum polycephalum found the shortest route to oat flakes, and Atsushi Tero's Tokyo map experiment matched the Tokyo rail network.

segments.title: Roman roads experiment and city planning
segments.summary: Oat flake experiments in the Balkans mimicked known and lost ancient Roman roads, and the hosts discuss whether slime molds could aid city planning.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break with banter about oat flakes.

segments.title: Bottom-up decision making, cAMP, and AI
segments.summary: Early researchers Evelyn Fox Keller and Lee Segel thought a leader cell directed slime mold aggregation, but the process is bottom-up, with cAMP signals passed from cells nearest food. The hosts link this to AI design and nanotechnology.

segments.title: Off-topic banter about Movie Crush and Jack
segments.summary: The hosts chat about Alfalfa Malina, a Movie Crush appearance by Miles, and an upcoming guest named Jack.

segments.title: Oscillating units, habituation, and memory
segments.summary: Plasmodial slime molds move via oscillating units. Experiments with a salt bridge show that habituated slime molds can teach naive ones to cross a harmless noxious substance, and that memory lasts about three hours of fusion.

segments.title: Cosmic web simulation and Sage Jensen
segments.summary: Sage Jensen turned slime mold algorithms into C++ code, and astrophysicists used a modified version to model 37,000 galaxies and the invisible filaments of the universe.

segments.title: Listener mail: Night Trap and Double Switch
segments.summary: Aaron from Michigan writes about the game Night Trap and suggests Double Switch, and the hosts respond about touring.
